386.title: Arousing
386.hook: waking good states not yet present
386.howItsDone: Buddhists cultivate wholesome qualities through daily practices such as meditation, chanting, generosity and keeping good company; teachers often stress the spiritual friend, kalyāṇamitta.

segments.voice: Yesterday: abandoning, five ways with a sticky thought, gentlest first. A finer peg pushes out a coarse one.

Patience with small children. Giving without keeping score. Staying calm when the flight is canceled and the line at the desk is shouting. People admire these qualities in a friend and wish they had them. They're easy to file under personality: some people got them, some didn't. The suttas file them somewhere else. The third of the four efforts is about exactly this: bringing into being good qualities that aren't there yet.
screen: `PATIENT WITH SMALL CHILDREN.` → `CALM AT THE CANCELED FLIGHT.` → `PERSONALITY, OR PRACTICE?`

segments.voice: The text is short: for wholesome states that haven't arisen, one generates desire, makes an effort, rouses energy, and strives for them to arise. The first step is desire, chanda: the wish to have the good thing. Buddhism is sometimes summed up as wanting nothing at all. The suttas are more careful. Wanting to grow in kindness or patience isn't the problem; it's the fuel. In the next sutta over, the Buddha says what this effort develops: the seven factors of awakening, mindfulness, investigation, energy, joy, tranquility, concentration and equanimity. So how do good states get started? The Book of Ones, the first section of the Numbered Discourses, keeps coming back to two sparks. One is wise attention: turning the mind toward things in a way that wakes the good. The other is good friendship: spending time with people who already have it. You don't grow patience by staring at the word. You grow it by noticing the small moments where patience is possible, and by being around patient people until it rubs off. Then the honest obstacle: inertia. The Dhammapada names it, in Max Müller's words: "He who does not rouse himself when it is time to rise" will not find the way. Arousing the good is mostly about starting, small, on one particular morning.
screen: `GOOD QUALITIES CAN BE GROWN.` · `CHANDA: THE WISH IS THE FUEL.` · `TWO SPARKS: ATTENTION AND FRIENDS.` · `A HABIT BEGINS AS ONE MORNING.` · then, large: `WAKE THE GOOD.`

segments.voice: Choose one good quality you'd like more of, patience, generosity, courage, and remember one moment, even a tiny one, when you had a little of it: where you were, how it felt in the body. That's wise attention, turning toward the seed; then picture the smallest way to practice it, just once.
Arousing. The third effort: bringing good states into being. The wish for the good, wise attention, and good friends are the sparks.
Your line: wake the good. The wish for the good is the fuel, not the problem. That's day three hundred eighty-six.

387.title: Maintaining
387.hook: keeping good states going and growing
387.howItsDone: Buddhist practitioners keep daily routines, a morning sit, evening chanting, regular offerings, and many traditions encourage rejoicing in one's own good deeds as a way of sustaining them.

segments.voice: Yesterday: arousing, bringing a good quality into being. Wake the good, starting small.

Day one of a new habit has the thrill of starting. Day two is just doing it again. No fanfare, no new pen. A beautiful journal gets three lovely pages, and six months later it turns up under the bed, the rest of it blank. Starting a good thing is the third effort. Keeping it going is the fourth, and for this one the Buddha reached for pictures from the farmyard and the workshop.
screen: `DAY ONE: THE THRILL.` → `DAY TWO: AGAIN.` → `THE JOURNAL UNDER THE BED.`

segments.voice: The fourth effort, in the Numbered Discourses, is for wholesome states already arisen: you work to keep them, so they don't fade or get muddled, and help them grow to fullness. The Pali name is anurakkhaṇā, protecting, guarding what you have. The list's own example is a meditator protecting a steady object of concentration once they've found it. But how do you keep at something without straining? A sutta in the Connected Discourses gives two pictures. A hen sits on her eggs, eight or ten or twelve, covering them, warming them, tending them properly. She doesn't need to wish, may my chicks break out today. If she keeps sitting, they will. Then a carpenter looks at the handle of his adze, a woodworking tool, and sees the marks his fingers have worn into it. He couldn't say how much wore away today, or yesterday. But it wore. Just so, the Buddha says, a monk can't see how much of the mind's taints wore away today, but steady practice wears them away. The Dhammapada adds the other half, in Max Müller's words: "If a man does what is good, let him do it again; let him delight in it: happiness is the outcome of good." Gladness isn't a distraction from keeping a good thing going. It's part of what keeps it going.

segments.voice: Bring back any good thing you've been doing lately, without measuring it or asking whether it's working. Picture yourself doing it again, the way a hen settles back onto her eggs, no fuss, no wishing, and let a little gladness come with the picture if it wants to.
Maintaining. Anurakkhaṇā, the fourth effort: keeping good states going and growing, like a hen sitting on her eggs.

388.title: The lute string
388.hook: Sona strains too hard; the Buddha asks how a lute sounds when its strings are too tight or too loose (AN 6.55)
388.howItsDone: Meditation teachers across Buddhist traditions tell Sona's story to students who push too hard or drift, and encourage them to adjust effort through a sit rather than force it.

segments.voice: Yesterday: maintaining, like a hen sitting on her eggs. Keep it going, and enjoy doing good again.

On the walking path in a forest called the Cool Grove, a young monk has been pacing back and forth for so long that his feet are bleeding. The path behind him is stained. His name is Sona. He grew up wealthy and sheltered, and he's decided to make up for it by trying harder than anyone else. And right in the middle of all that effort, he's thinking about quitting. On day twenty you met the image at the heart of this story. Today, the whole story.
screen: `THE COOL GROVE.` → `PACING UNTIL HIS FEET BLEED.` → `THINKING OF QUITTING.`

segments.voice: Sona's thought, the sutta says, runs like this: I'm one of the most energetic of the Buddha's disciples, and still my mind isn't free. My family has wealth. I could go home, enjoy it, and do good with it. The Buddha knows what he's thinking and comes to him. He doesn't scold or push. He asks about music. Sona, before you went forth, weren't you skilled at the lute? Yes, sir. When its strings were too tight, did it sound right? No, sir. Too loose? No, sir. And tuned to an even pitch, neither too tight nor too loose? Then it sounded right, sir. Just so, the Buddha says: effort that's too strong leads to restlessness, and effort that's too slack leads to laziness. Settle on an even pitch of effort, and tune the rest of your practice to it. The vīṇā, the Indian lute, isn't a random choice. Sona knows it with his hands; the Buddha teaches him in the language of his own skill. And it matters for the four efforts. Effort isn't a dial that only turns up. Some days the string is slack, and you need to rouse yourself. Some days it's wound so tight it buzzes, and you need to ease off. The sutta says Sona took this to heart, practiced with balance, and before long became an arahant, fully awakened. The walking path stayed the same. The tuning changed.
screen: `TRYING HARDER THAN ANYONE.` · `TOO TIGHT, TOO LOOSE.` · `THE EVEN PITCH OF EFFORT.` · `EASE OFF, OR TURN IT UP.` · then, large: `TUNE THE STRING.`

segments.voice: Check the string: if the body is tight, jaw set, shoulders up, ease it a quarter turn and let the breath happen; if it's slack and drifting, sit up a little and feel the breath more clearly. Keep tuning gently through the sit, a little looser, a little tighter, listening for the even note.
Vina, the Indian lute. The Buddha's lesson for Sona: effort too tight brings restlessness, too loose brings laziness. Tune it to an even pitch.
Your line: tune the string. Too tight brings restlessness; too loose brings laziness. Day three hundred eighty-eight, done.

389.title: Right mindfulness
389.hook: the four foundations, now as a factor of the path (MN 141)
389.howItsDone: Buddhists practice right mindfulness through satipaṭṭhāna meditation, often beginning with the breath, and through attention carried into daily activity; in Theravada the Satipaṭṭhāna Sutta is widely chanted and studied.

segments.voice: Yesterday: the vina, Sona's lute. Tune the string, neither too tight nor too loose.

In the Deer Park near Benares, where he first taught, the Buddha gives his monks a brief summary of the four noble truths. Then he praises Sariputta and Moggallana, says Sariputta can explain the truths in detail, gets up, and goes into his dwelling. It's one of the moments the canon records him handing the teaching to a student. Sariputta takes it from there, truth by truth, factor by factor, and when he reaches the seventh factor of the path, he defines it in one long, careful sentence.
screen: `THE DEER PARK, AGAIN.` → `A BRIEF SUMMARY.` → `SARIPUTTA TAKES IT FROM THERE.`

segments.voice: Sammā sati. Sati is usually translated mindfulness, but it corresponds to the Sanskrit smṛti, memory. So mindfulness here is less like a spotlight and more like remembering: remembering to notice, remembering what you're doing while you're doing it. Sariputta's sentence runs like this. A practitioner dwells contemplating the body as body, ardent, clearly knowing and mindful, having set aside wanting and grief about the world. Then feelings as feelings. The mind as mind. And dhammas, the patterns of experience, as dhammas. Four foundations; the first year spent three weeks on them. What's new is where they sit. On their own, they're a meditation method. As the seventh factor of the path, they're a working part of something larger. Right view tells mindfulness what to look for. Right effort supplies the energy to keep looking. Right concentration, later on the path, gathers what mindfulness has noticed into stillness. And in the great forty sutta, where three factors circle around each of the others, mindfulness is one of the three: it's there inside right speech, right action, right livelihood, all of it. That's why the line is so plain. Not a special state you visit on a cushion, but a habit of remembering, in an ordinary day, that you're here, in a body, feeling something, thinking something, and that you can see it.
screen: `SATI: ROOTED IN MEMORY.` · `BODY, FEELINGS, MIND, DHAMMAS.` · `A WORKING PART OF THE PATH.` · `REMEMBERING THAT YOU'RE HERE.` · then, large: `REMEMBER TO NOTICE.`

segments.voice: Touch all four foundations, about half a minute each: the body where it meets the seat; whether this moment feels pleasant, unpleasant or neither; the mind, calm or restless, sleepy or bright; and whatever pattern is here, a wanting, a pushing away, some ease. Each time you drift, remembering is the practice, and if you have five minutes afterward, stay.
Sammā sati. Right mindfulness: the four foundations, body, feelings, mind and dhammas, as the seventh factor of the path.
Your line: remember to notice. Mindfulness is a habit of remembering, not a place you visit. See you tomorrow.

390.title: The gatekeeper
390.hook: mindfulness is like the wise gatekeeper of a frontier fortress (AN 7, the fortress)
390.howItsDone: Meditation teachers often use the gatekeeper image to describe mindfulness as noticing and naming what arises, and some traditions practice mental noting, labeling each thought or feeling as it appears.

segments.voice: Yesterday: samma sati, right mindfulness. Remember to notice: body, feelings, mind, and the patterns of experience.

At the edge of a kingdom, where the road comes in from foreign land, stands a fortress. Thick walls. A moat. Soldiers. Storerooms of grain and oil. And at the gate, one person whose whole job is to look at every face that arrives and decide: you, come in; you, I don't know you, wait outside. Everything inside depends on that one person paying attention. The Buddha drew this fortress in detail, piece by piece.
screen: `A FORTRESS ON THE FRONTIER.` → `WALLS, MOAT, SOLDIERS, STORES.` → `ONE PERSON AT THE GATE.`

segments.voice: The sutta is in the book of sevens of the Numbered Discourses. A king's frontier fortress, the Buddha says, can't be taken by enemies from outside when it has seven things in place and four kinds of provisions stored. Then he maps each piece onto a practitioner. The deep-rooted pillar at the entrance is faith. The moat is a sense of shame about doing wrong. The path patrolled around the walls is fear of wrongdoing. The weapons are learning, the teachings you've heard. The army is energy. The high, thick rampart is wisdom. And the gatekeeper, wise, experienced and intelligent, who keeps strangers out and lets known friends in, is mindfulness. He doesn't fight; that's the army's job. He doesn't build the walls. He knows who's who, and he's at his post. That's anger, coming up the road. That's kindness, a friend: open the gate. Without him, the strongest walls are useless; the enemy simply walks in, because no one noticed. A few days ago you guarded the sense doors. This is the same gate, seen from inside the walls, and it echoes a Dhammapada line from the first year, in Max Müller's words: "Like a well-guarded frontier fort, with defences within and without, so let a man guard himself." A frontier fort, not a palace: mindfulness stands where ordinary life arrives.
screen: `SEVEN DEFENSES, FOUR STORES.` · `PILLAR, MOAT, WEAPONS, ARMY, WALL.` · `THE GATEKEEPER KNOWS WHO'S WHO.` · `WHERE ORDINARY LIFE ARRIVES.` · then, large: `THE GATEKEEPER.`

segments.voice: Picture yourself at the gate as thoughts and moods come up the road, and name each one as it arrives: worry, planning, a memory, irritation, tenderness. Don't fight any of them; let the friendly ones in, let the strangers wait outside, and stay at your post.
The gatekeeper. In the book of sevens, mindfulness is the wise gatekeeper of the frontier fortress, the one who knows who's who.
Your line: know who's who. The gatekeeper doesn't fight; he recognizes. Three hundred ninety days now.

391.title: The bowl of oil
391.hook: carry a full bowl of oil past a crowd and a dancing beauty, a swordsman behind you (SN 47.20)
391.howItsDone: Many Buddhists practice mindfulness of the body in walking meditation and daily tasks, and some teachers have students carry a full cup or bowl slowly as a training in steady attention.

segments.voice: Yesterday: the gatekeeper, mindfulness at the fortress gate, letting friends in and keeping strangers out. Know who's who.

A huge crowd is gathering in the town square. Word has spread: the most beautiful woman in the land is here, and she's dancing and singing. People are pushing to see. Now a man is handed a bowl filled to the very brim with oil, and told to carry it straight through the middle of all that, between the crowd and the dancer. Behind him walks another man, with a drawn sword. Spill one drop, he's told, and you lose your head.
screen: `THE CROWD PUSHES TO SEE.` → `A BOWL FULL TO THE BRIM.` → `A DRAWN SWORD BEHIND.`

segments.voice: The Buddha tells this at Sedaka, the same town as the acrobats, and asks his monks a simple question. Would that man stop paying attention to the bowl, and let his eyes drift to the dancer? No, sir, they say. Then he says what the picture means. The bowl of oil filled to the brim stands for mindfulness of the body. So train yourselves, he says, to develop mindfulness of the body, to make it your vehicle and your ground. The picture is extreme on purpose. The crowd and the dancer are everything that pulls attention outward: the alerts, the drama, the bright, loud, lovely things. The sutta doesn't explain the sword, but one way to read it is as the seriousness of the stakes. Not that distraction is a crime; just that it may cost more than it seems. And the bowl is the body itself: the breath, the feet, the hands, right here, the thing you're already carrying. The man doesn't shut his eyes. He doesn't stay home. He walks straight through the crowd while the music plays. The practice isn't avoiding life; it's carrying something steady through the middle of it. That's right mindfulness at its most physical: attention in your hands, at the brim of the bowl, step by step, while everything around you invites you to look away.
screen: `WOULD HE LOOK AWAY?` · `THE BOWL: MINDFULNESS OF THE BODY.` · `THE SWORD: THE STAKES ARE REAL.` · `THROUGH THE CROWD, NOT AROUND IT.` · then, large: `DON'T SPILL.`

segments.voice: If you can, fill a cup to the top and hold it, or imagine one in your hands, and slowly carry it a few steps, or raise and lower it, without spilling. Notice how the whole body gathers around the brim, the breath slowing, the hands softening, then set it down and sit with that same steadiness.
Kayagata sati, mindfulness of the body. The Buddha's image for mindfulness of the body: carried brim-full through the crowd, without spilling.
Your line: don't spill. The bowl is the body you're already carrying. That's day three hundred ninety-one.

392.title: Six animals
392.hook: a snake, crocodile, bird, dog, jackal and monkey tied to one post: the body as the post (SN 35.247)
392.howItsDone: Many Buddhists practice mindfulness of the body by returning attention to posture and breath through the day, in walking as well as sitting meditation; teachers in several schools describe the body as an anchor for the wandering mind.

segments.voice: Yesterday: kayagata sati, mindfulness of the body, carried like a brim-full bowl through the crowd. Don't spill.

A man walks into a clearing with six animals on six ropes. A snake. A crocodile. A bird. A dog. A jackal. A monkey. He knots the six ropes together in the middle, and lets go. The snake heads for its anthill. The crocodile for the river. The bird for the sky, the dog for the village, the jackal for the charnel ground, the monkey for the forest. Six directions, one knot, and whoever is strongest drags the rest.
screen: `SIX ANIMALS, SIX ROPES.` → `SIX DIRECTIONS, ONE KNOT.` → `THE STRONGEST DRAGS THE REST.`

segments.voice: The story comes from the Connected Discourses, in the book on the six senses, and the Buddha tells it twice. The first time, the ropes are only tied to each other, and the others get dragged after whichever animal is strongest. Then he tells it again with a single change. The man ties all six ropes to a strong post, driven deep into the ground. The animals pull just as hard. The snake still wants its anthill. The monkey still wants its forest. Nobody has been tamed. But the post doesn't move. After a while, worn out, they stand by the post, then sit down by it, then lie down beside it. The six animals are the six senses: eye, ear, nose, tongue, body and mind, each pulling toward what it likes and away from what it doesn't. The post is mindfulness directed to the body, kayagata sati: knowing you're sitting while you sit, breathing while you breathe. The Buddha doesn't say kill the animals, or blindfold the eye. The senses keep their nature. What changes is that there's something steady to be tied to. Under right mindfulness, the seventh factor of the path, mindfulness isn't a mood. It's a post. Some teachers put it this way: the body is always here; it's the mind that runs off to the anthill and the forest. And that ends a week: waking the good, keeping it going, the lute string, remembering to notice, the gatekeeper, the bowl of oil, and six animals with something to be tied to.
screen: `TIED ONLY TO EACH OTHER.` · `THE SAME ANIMALS, TIED TO A POST.` · `SIX ANIMALS, SIX SENSES.` · `THE POST: MINDFULNESS OF THE BODY.` · then, large: `THE POST HOLDS.`

segments.voice: Find the post first: your feet, the weight of your body on the seat, your hands where they rest. Then let the animals pull, a sound, a thought about tomorrow, an itch, and each time, notice which one is pulling and come back to the weight of the body; coming back to the feet on the floor is coming back to the post.
Six animals. The six senses, each pulling toward its own place, tied to one steady post: mindfulness of the body.
Your line: the post holds. The animals keep their nature, and the post doesn't move. A week done: day three hundred ninety-two.

myth: in the story, the Buddha says to get rid of the six animals
the animals keep their nature; tied to a post, they pull until they tire and lie down.

eye, ear, nose, tongue, body and mind: each pulls toward its own range.

fork.setup: you've tied six animals to a strong post driven deep into the ground. they pull in six directions. what happens, in the Buddha's story?
options: the post breaks
they pull, tire, and lie down beside the post
the strongest drags the others away
fork.reveal: the post doesn't move. worn out, the animals stand, then sit, then lie down beside it. the senses aren't destroyed; they're given something steady.

original.note: Pali saḷāyatana: the six sense bases, eye, ear, nose, tongue, body and mind, which the six animals stand for.

trapdoor: what you thought: a list of animals to make a point about distraction.
what it means: six senses, each with its own pull, and one steady post that lets them settle.

what a scholar hears: the post is named kāyagatā sati, mindfulness directed to the body; the sutta is numbered SN 35.247 in Bhikkhu Bodhi's edition and SN 35.206 in the older Pali Text Society numbering.
guess: the six senses, each pulling its own way
six rebirths a being passes through
six wild urges a monk has to kill off

chat.says: Does mindfulness mean shutting your senses off?
options: No: the senses keep pulling, but tied to a steady post, they settle down.
Yes, you blindfold the eye and stop the ear until nothing pulls.
No, you just follow whichever sense pulls hardest at the moment.
chat.meaning: In SN 35.247 the six animals are the six senses; tied to the post of mindfulness of the body, they tire and lie down.
